title: Sancocho Dominicano
subtitle: Dominican root vegetable and chicken stew with corn
excerpt: A hearty Dominican stew built from chicken, yuca, plantain, West Indian yam and corn, slow-cooked until the broth is deep and golden. This recipe serves 8 and takes about 2 hours. Sancocho is a dish of celebration in the Dominican Republic, traditionally cooked outdoors in large pots for family gatherings.
sourceNotes: Sancocho is eaten across the Caribbean and Latin America in many local variations. The Dominican version is one of the heartiest, using multiple root vegetables including yuca, plantain and name. It is a dish of celebration and gatherings, traditionally cooked outdoors over a wood fire for Dominican national holidays and family reunions.

recipe.freezeNotes: Freeze for up to 2 months. Root vegetables may soften further on reheating.
recipe.batchNotes: Sancocho is traditionally cooked in large pots for gatherings. Scale up freely.

content.text: This recipe serves 8 and takes about 2 hours. Sancocho is a slow-cooked stew and is not one to rush. The broth deepens in flavour as the root vegetables soften into it, and the chicken becomes tender enough to shred easily. Start it early in the day and it will be ready by the time people are hungry.

Yuca (cassava), name (West Indian yam) and green plantain are all available in Afro-Caribbean and Latin American food shops. If you cannot find name, substitute sweet potato, though the flavour is different. Achiote oil or annatto seeds give the broth its warm golden colour; if you cannot find these, a pinch of turmeric does a similar job on colour without adding any flavour. Season as you go and taste at the end: the broth should be savoury, lightly herby and with a good depth from the chicken.
Put the chicken pieces in a large pot. Add the garlic, onion, and 1.5 litres of water. Bring to the boil and skim the foam. Reduce the heat and simmer for 20 minutes.
Heat the oil in a very large pot over medium-high heat. Brown the chicken thighs in batches, 3 to 4 minutes per side, until golden. Remove and set aside.

In the same pot, fry the onion for 5 minutes until softened. Add the garlic and diced tomatoes, stir and cook for 3 minutes. Stir in 1 tbsp achiote oil or a pinch of annatto seeds if using, for colour.
Return the chicken to the pot. Add 2.5 litres of cold water, the bunch of coriander and 1 chicken stock cube. Bring to the boil, skim any foam, then reduce to a simmer and cook for 30 minutes.

Peel and cut 300g yuca (cassava) into chunks, removing the fibrous core. Cut 2 green plantains into rounds. Peel and cut 300g name or sweet potato into large chunks. Cut 2 ears of corn into rounds. Add all the vegetables to the pot.

Simmer for a further 45 to 50 minutes until all the root vegetables are tender and the broth has a good depth of flavour. Remove the coriander bunch. Taste and adjust the seasoning generously with salt.
Serve in deep bowls with white rice on the side, a squeeze of lime and fresh coriander scattered over. Pass the lime wedges at the table.

attrs.symptom: Yuca is stringy and hard to eat
attrs.cause: The fibrous core was not removed, or the yuca was not cooked for long enough
attrs.fix: After peeling yuca, cut each piece in half and remove the thin woody core running through the centre. If it is still tough after 45 minutes of simmering, continue cooking until a fork passes through easily.

attrs.symptom: Broth is thin and lacks flavour
attrs.cause: Not enough seasoning or the chicken was not browned first
attrs.fix: Browning the chicken properly before adding water creates the foundation of the broth. Add an extra stock cube and more adobo seasoning. Simmer uncovered for 15 minutes to concentrate the broth.

attrs.symptom: Root vegetables have turned to mush
attrs.cause: Cooked for too long or cut too small
attrs.fix: Cut all root vegetables into large pieces (at least 4cm). If the broth is done but the vegetables are very soft, ladle them out carefully before serving to avoid breaking them up further.

content.text: In the Dominican Republic, sancocho is the dish you make when there is something to celebrate. Independence Day, a family reunion, a quinceañera: the pot goes on early and the whole neighbourhood smells of it by midday. It is always cooked in bulk, always shared and always better the next day after the broth has rested overnight. Dominican families living abroad make it when they want to feel at home.
